I can then notice that the thought of this being contains the idea of a “God” whose existence is necessarily independent of whether I think about him.
Everything else—including the axioms of mathematics—can still be doubted.
But, Descartes says, since “God” exists and is a perfect being, he cannot deceive me.
So whatever I perceive as “clearly and distinctly” as I perceive my own existence must be true.
But if it is true, it is not simply because it is clear. It is true because God cannot allow me to be mistaken about what appears clear to me. Otherwise he would be a deceptive God.
Whether this reasoning is wrong does not matter much for our present purpose.
What matters is that, for Descartes, human self-knowledge stops almost as soon as it begins and can proceed again only by appealing to “God.”
What we needed to establish was what follows from Descartes’s unsupported identification of the being of the I with the being of a thing.
If my I is a thing, then it possesses unchanging qualities. And if it does not possess “wisdom” now, it will never possess it. It will doubt forever.
If that is so, then we have to place “wisdom” outside humanity.
In other words, we have to assume the existence of God.
We still do not know why the I does not exist in the way a thing does. We will see that soon.

But even now we can say that it is wrong to identify the I with a thing, because that identification leads with logical necessity to the false conclusions that the soul is immortal and that God exists.
For the moment, though, that is not our main concern.
We brought up Descartes because we wanted to know what, according to him, a human being needs to know in general in order to speak about himself and to know how to answer questions about himself.
On the one hand, Descartes implies that a person can know everything that matters about himself without knowing anything about the world, including his own body.
Self-consciousness, on this view, neither presupposes nor includes knowledge of the world.
This is obviously a claim of enormous importance. It means that the philosopher who wants to know himself can ignore the world, “withdraw” from it, “shut himself up within himself,” and so on.
In short, he can renounce all “worldly” activity.
On the other hand, Descartes assumes that a person’s knowledge of himself cannot develop without knowledge of God.
But the important point is that, given his starting assumption, Descartes is entirely right about both of these things.
If we assume that my thinking I exists as a thing, as a “soul,” then knowledge of a human being—that is, of his “soul”—will indeed depend not on knowledge of the world but on knowledge of God.
The result of our entire examination of Descartes can therefore be stated like this.
If we identify the human I with a thing, treating it as a “soul,” then we must assume that a person’s knowledge of himself is not all knowledge but only one part of it.
To answer questions about oneself, one does not need to be able to answer every possible question.
In particular, one might be unable to answer questions about the world, although one would have to be able to answer questions about God.
There is nothing obviously wrong with saying that a human being can know himself without knowing everything.
A philosopher might even say: so much the better.
Certainly, cutting humanity off from the world looks unacceptable. But we do not yet know that a relation to the world is necessary for human existence.
Bringing knowledge of God into our knowledge of ourselves is certainly unfortunate. But, after all, we do not yet know that God does not exist.
So if we begin only with philosophy’s conception of its own goal—that is, with the demand for the fullest possible knowledge of oneself—we cannot yet object to Descartes’s conclusion.
Our objections begin only when it becomes clear that, because he starts from the assumption that the human I is a “thing,” the knowledge we gain of it is inevitably inadequate.
That is what we now have to show.
Let us recall how Descartes answers his first philosophical question, “Who am I?” or, more precisely, “What am I?”
He then goes on, with the help of God’s “guarantee,” to explain what properties this “thinking being” has.
We need not examine those properties here.
It is enough to notice that Descartes’s answer is philosophically inadequate for the simple reason that he keeps talking about a thinking being in general, not about himself.
You can finish reading his book and still know almost nothing about who Descartes himself actually was: a Frenchman living in the seventeenth century who led a particular life.
In other words, once he begins philosophizing in this way, Descartes becomes clearly incapable of answering questions about his own life and activity.

That is hardly surprising. He believes that one can speak about a human being without speaking about the world, while at the same time he knows perfectly well that the life and activity of the historical Descartes would have been impossible without that world.
We ask Descartes who he is, and he replies: “a thinking being.”

It is as though we asked an engineer what some exceptionally complicated machine was and he solemnly replied, “It is iron,” before launching into a lecture on the chemical and physical properties of that metal.
Even if everything he said about iron were completely correct—which certainly cannot be said of Descartes’s account of the “soul”—we would still find the answer completely unsatisfactory.
We asked about this machine. And about this machine, we have learned almost nothing.
The same is true of Descartes.
We ask who he is, and he gives us the definition of a certain “thinking being.” We have learned nothing about him.
In fact, Descartes’s philosophical answer is even less satisfactory than the engineer’s.
A machine is certainly more than iron. But it really may be made of iron. So by learning the properties of iron, we have at least learned something about the machine.
But you could never construct Descartes—or even a human being in general—out of what our philosopher calls a “thinking thing.”
Experience shows that human beings not only always live in the world but are bound to it in the most concrete way.
On the one hand, their consciousness is shaped by their worldly existence.
On the other, through thought and work they change the world in which they live.

The Cartesian I, the “thinking thing,” is supposed to be completely independent of the world. It therefore cannot change as the real conditions of life change, and it cannot transform those conditions either.
Even if we grant that the Cartesian I can think, it is clearly incapable of working.
And an I that does not work and cannot work has almost nothing in common with the human I.
Experience also shows us that the human I is essentially historical.
Human beings were very different thousands of years ago from what they are today.
A pagan Greek lived and acted in a fundamentally different way from a medieval Christian, who in turn differs essentially from the modern bourgeois.
But the Cartesian I, endowed once and for all with fixed and unchanging qualities, plainly cannot change.
It is as independent of the human world—the social, political, and historical world—as it is of the natural world.

Yet what characterizes the human I is precisely that its qualities are shaped, on the one hand, by historical conditions and, on the other, by social and political activity and struggle that alter and create those very conditions.
A “thinking thing” incapable of struggle resembles a human being no more than a “thinking thing” incapable of work.
So this Cartesian “thinking thing” cannot give us a living human being, still less Descartes himself.
And that should not surprise us, because nothing Descartes says about this “thing” explains his own life.
Descartes is not the particular person he is simply because he thinks.
What makes him Descartes rather than someone else is a particular way of living. He not only thinks; he also writes and publishes what he writes.
Why does he live in this way rather than another?
Why does he not merely think, but also put his thoughts on paper?
Why does he not merely write them down, but publish them?
Why does he publish some manuscripts and burn others?
We have to admit that his reflections on himself—or rather, on the “thinking thing”—give us no answer to any of these questions.

The definition of the human I as a thinking thing is therefore plainly inadequate from a philosophical point of view. It cannot answer the questions we can ask a philosopher about his life and activity in the real world.
It follows logically from Descartes’s original decision to define the I as a thinking being—that is, as a thing, a “soul.”

If our I really is a “soul,” a thing-like being or “substance,” an unchanging hypokeimenon or underlying substance that remains beneath all our changes and actions, then like any other “thing” it must possess qualities that depend only on itself.
That means a human being’s qualities cannot depend on the natural world, including the body, or be constantly shaped through interaction with that world.

A soul shut up within itself therefore becomes infinitely poorer in qualities than a real human being, whose character is shaped by the immense variety of natural conditions in which life takes place.

From Descartes’s point of view, for example, Inuit people, Europeans, and Africans may live in very different ways because their bodies differ in certain respects. But everything genuinely human in them must be perfectly identical.
This leaves it impossible to explain why they differ not only in appearance but also in what they think and say.
If a human being is a “soul” or a “thing,” all of his essential qualities must be completely unchanging.

From Descartes’s point of view, there can therefore be no genuinely human difference between people living in ancient lake settlements and people living in American skyscrapers. Why the former do not think exactly like the latter becomes impossible to explain.

So this view strips human beings not only of the richness and variety produced by the different natural conditions in which they live, but also of the richness and variety produced by different historical conditions.
More generally, once philosophy defines the human I as a “soul-thing,” it is inevitably driven toward an extremely impoverished and simplified picture of humanity.

If we assume that the I is a “soul,” possessing from eternity unchanging qualities that belong only to itself—rather like the fixed properties of some perfectly tangible object—then only two possibilities remain.
Either all human beings are fundamentally identical, and the differences between them are merely superficial and have no real significance.
Or there are as many different “souls” as there are human beings.

But if every human being has a completely different soul, then the concept of “soul” loses all meaning. We might as well speak directly about living people. “Soul” would become nothing more than an extra, unnecessary word for a person.
And then there could be no general discourse or science of humanity—no anthropology.
We could speak only about isolated individuals.
Anything I could say about myself would interest no one except me, since it would apply to no one else.
Philosophy would then become a purely private and idle pastime.

But if, by contrast, we say that all human beings are essentially identical, we must either deny their physiological differences despite the obvious evidence, or declare those differences philosophically irrelevant.

And then everything that matters to actual flesh-and-blood human beings—intelligence and stupidity, decency and immorality, energy and apathy, political convictions, national differences, and so on—gets thrown overboard from the ship of “philosophy.”
Philosophy then becomes a “science” completely detached from life, one that ordinary people have no reason to care about.

If my philosophy—my answer to the question of who I am—is to have a genuinely common meaning and to interest other people, then the answers I give about myself must also tell us something about humanity in general.
